title: Travel Tracker Part 3
summary: Optional polish for the Travel Tracker: wrap the queries in try/catch so bad or duplicate countries show an error in the input placeholder, and make the lookup forgiving with LOWER, LIKE and || so partial or differently cased names match.

concepts.heading: Edge cases being fixed
points: Unknown country name: Part 2 either hangs or crashes. Goal: re-show the page with the placeholder saying the country does not exist.
Duplicate country: inserting an already-saved code violates the UNIQUE constraint on country_code. Goal: placeholder says it was already added.
Long official names: Tanzania is stored under a longer official name, so exact matching fails even though the country is valid.
These are optional; solution3.js covers error handling and solution4.js adds the fuzzy lookup.

concepts.heading: Error handling with try/catch (solution3)
points: index.ejs already shows the placeholder as the error value if an error variable exists (locals.error), otherwise the default prompt. So the server only needs to pass error.
Outer try wraps the lookup SELECT from countries and reading rows[0].country_code. If no row exists, rows[0] is undefined and reading its property throws, which lands in the outer catch.
Outer catch: log the error, fetch visited countries with the helper function, and res.render index.ejs with countries, total and error 'Country name does not exist, try again.'
Inner try wraps the INSERT into visited_countries. A UNIQUE violation throws and the inner catch renders the page with an 'already added' message.
In the error path use res.render, not res.redirect, because the error value has to be passed to the template; a redirect would drop it.
The helper that returns the visited codes is reused here so the map and total still display correctly alongside the error.

concepts.heading: Fuzzy, case-insensitive lookup (solution4)
points: Replace the equality check with LOWER(country_name) LIKE '%' || $1 || '%'. The || joins wildcards to both sides of the placeholder, so the input may appear anywhere in the stored name.
Pass input.toLowerCase() as the parameter, and wrap the column in SQL LOWER() so both sides are lowercase and casing is irrelevant.
This is the reason to know the || form from the LIKE lesson: the pattern includes a variable that is not a literal.

(Extra) A short input such as 'a' or 'in' will now match many countries and only the first row is used, so results can be surprising; ordering or an exact-match-first query would be a further refinement.
General lesson: find edge cases while testing, then fix them one at a time with more precise SQL and better error handling.

task.name: Travel Tracker Part 3: error handling and fuzzy matching (optional)
task.starting_point: The working Part 2 app (solution2.js), plus solution3.js and solution4.js to compare.
task.goal: Show a helpful message for unknown or duplicate countries, and let Tanzania (or a lowercase name) match the stored value.
steps: Wrap the lookup query in try/catch; in the catch, log, fetch visited countries and render index.ejs with an error 'does not exist'.
Wrap the INSERT in its own try/catch; in the catch render with an 'already added' error.
Test by entering a nonsense name and re-adding a visited country; the input placeholder should change.
Change the lookup to LOWER(country_name) LIKE '%' || $1 || '%' and pass input.toLowerCase().
Test with Tanzania and with lowercase input.
task.expected_result: Bad or duplicate entries leave the map intact and show a message; Tanzania is accepted.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 33 - PostgreSQL/33.10 - Travel Tracker Part 3/Travel Tracker/solution4.js

pitfalls: Using res.redirect on error, which loses the error value.
Forgetting that rows[0] is undefined for no match, so the thrown TypeError is what triggers the catch.
Passing the original-case input while lowercasing only one side of the comparison.
Leaving out the % wildcards so LIKE behaves like equality.
Very short inputs matching unintended countries.

gaps_and_ideas: Could be folded into the Travel Tracker lesson series as a final 'edge cases' lesson.
Tasks: add try/catch with a user-visible error, handle duplicates, make the lookup case-insensitive, find an input that matches too many rows.
Starter idea: mock query function that throws for unknown or duplicate codes.
Interactive demo: type a name and watch a mock lookup table highlight rows matched by exact, LIKE and LOWER+LIKE modes.
